lessons.title: What first line maintenance is
lessons.html:
The operator's role in maintenance

First line maintenance is the routine care that operators and supervisors carry out on their own equipment: inspecting, cleaning, lubricating, adjusting, tightening and replacing simple wear parts. It is the first defence against breakdowns. Major repairs, electrical work and anything beyond your training are done by qualified artisans.

In an abattoir this may include conveyors, carcass splitting saws, hide pullers, chain hoists, rail trolleys, knife sterilisers, hand wash stations, pumps and compressors. In a poultry or meat processing plant, it includes shackle lines, pluckers, mincers and packaging machines.

Why it matters

  • Prevents unplanned breakdowns that stop the whole line.
  • Keeps equipment hygienic: worn seals and cracked surfaces harbour bacteria.
  • Prevents physical contamination from loose bolts, broken parts or excess grease.
  • Improves safety: worn chains, frayed cables and missing guards cause injuries.
  • Extends equipment life and reduces costs.

Types of maintenance

TypeDescription
PreventivePlanned tasks at set intervals, such as daily lubrication and weekly belt checks
Condition-basedActing on signs such as noise, heat, vibration or wear
CorrectiveRepairing after a fault occurs

Know your limits

Only do tasks you have been trained and authorised to do. If the job involves electrical panels, refrigeration systems, pressure vessels, welding or structural repairs, call maintenance. If in doubt, stop and ask.

Information you need

  • Manufacturer's manual and lubrication chart
  • Maintenance schedule and checklist
  • Lockout procedure for the machine
  • Approved lubricants and parts list

lessons.title: Safe preparation and lockout
lessons.html:
Safety before any maintenance

Most maintenance injuries happen because a machine starts unexpectedly or stored energy is released. Every first line maintenance task begins with making the equipment safe.

Lockout and tagout steps

  1. Prepare: know what energy sources the machine has: electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, mechanical (springs, gravity), thermal (hot water, steam).
  2. Notify affected people that the machine will be shut down.
  3. Shut down using normal stop controls.
  4. Isolate all energy sources at the isolator, valve or disconnect.
  5. Lock and tag: fit your personal lock and a tag with your name, date and reason. Each person working on the machine fits their own lock.
  6. Release stored energy: bleed air or hydraulic pressure, lower or block raised parts, allow hot parts to cool.
  7. Verify: try the start button to confirm the machine cannot start, then return the control to off.

Never remove another person's lock. Only remove your lock when you have finished, all guards are back, tools are removed and people are clear.

Personal protective equipment

  • Safety boots and overalls or work clothes
  • Gloves suited to the task, such as cut-resistant for blades or chemical-resistant for cleaning
  • Safety glasses when using compressed air, grinding or working overhead
  • Hearing protection in noisy areas

Hygiene during maintenance

In food areas, maintenance must not contaminate product. Remove or cover product nearby, use food-grade lubricants where there is any chance of contact with food, count tools and parts in and out, and clean and sanitise the area and equipment before production restarts. Get the area signed off by the supervisor or quality controller if your plant requires it.

lessons.title: Inspecting, lubricating, adjusting and reporting
lessons.html:
Carrying out the tasks

Inspection

Use your senses and a checklist:

  • Look for leaks, cracks, wear, loose fasteners, frayed belts, missing guards, worn chain links and damaged seals.
  • Listen for unusual noises: squealing belts, grinding bearings, knocking.
  • Feel (only when safely isolated and cooled) for excessive heat or play in bearings and shafts.
  • Smell for burning insulation or overheated oil.

Lubrication

  • Use only the lubricant specified on the lubrication chart; food-grade where required.
  • Clean the grease nipple before applying grease so dirt is not pushed into the bearing.
  • Apply the specified amount. Over-greasing can damage seals and drip onto product.
  • Check oil levels in gearboxes against the sight glass or dipstick and top up with the correct grade.
  • Wipe off excess and dispose of rags and old oil according to the waste procedure.

Adjustments and minor replacements

Typical first line tasks include tensioning belts and chains to the manufacturer's specification, tightening loose bolts, replacing worn scraper blades, saw blades, gaskets or filters, and replacing damaged hoses on wash-down systems. Use the right tools and correct parts. Never improvise with wire, cable ties or non-approved parts in food areas.

Testing and handover

  1. Refit all guards and covers.
  2. Remove tools, rags and loose parts; count them.
  3. Clean and sanitise as required.
  4. Remove your lock following the procedure and restore energy.
  5. Test run the equipment and observe for correct operation.
  6. Hand back to production.

Recording and reporting

Record what was done, parts used, readings taken and any problems found on the maintenance checklist or job card. Report faults beyond your scope to maintenance with a clear description: machine, location, symptoms, when it started and urgency.

Key points

  • First line maintenance is routine inspecting, cleaning, lubricating and adjusting by trained operators.
  • Always isolate, lock, tag, release stored energy and verify before starting.
  • Never remove another person's lock.
  • Use the specified, food-grade lubricants and correct parts.
  • Refit guards, count tools and clean the area before handing back.
  • Record work done and report faults beyond your scope.
